questions.prompt: According to Jorgensen, how do discrete mathematics and graph theory divide between the main testing approaches?
options: Discrete math is more applicable to functional testing; graph theory to structural testing
Discrete math is more applicable to structural testing; graph theory to functional testing
Discrete math applies to unit testing; graph theory applies only to system testing
Both mainly support structural testing; functional testing needs no mathematics
Both mainly model continuous behavior, as calculus does for developers
questions.explanation: The book states that discrete mathematics is more applicable to functional testing, while graph theory pertains more to structural testing; the reversed pairing is the tempting trap.

questions.prompt: In Jorgensen's set theory section, a set can be defined in three ways. Which list gives them?
options: Listing its elements, giving a decision rule, or constructing it from other sets
Listing its elements, drawing a Venn diagram, or stating its cardinality
Giving a decision rule, computing its power set, or taking its complement
Listing its elements, naming its universe of discourse, or giving a partition
Constructing it from other sets, writing a truth table, or stating a proposition
questions.explanation: A set is defined by simply listing its elements, by giving a decision rule, or by constructing it from other sets; Venn diagrams only picture sets and cardinality is a property of a set.

questions.prompt: Testers often meet "untestable requirements", such as N = {t : t is a nearly equilateral triangle}. What does Jorgensen give as the usual reason such requirements cannot be tested?
options: They boil down to an ambiguous decision rule
Their decision rule is always false, so the set is empty
Their sets are infinite and cannot be drawn as Venn diagrams
Their elements are listed in no particular order
Their decision rule refers to itself, like the Barber of Seville
questions.explanation: Jorgensen says the reason such requirements cannot be tested often boils down to an ambiguous decision rule (is a (50, 50, 51) triangle nearly equilateral?); self-reference is a separate problem with very little application for testers.

questions.prompt: Which set is defined by the decision rule {year : 2012 ≤ year ≤ 1812}?
options: The empty set, because the decision rule is always false
All years from 1812 to 2012 inclusive
The two-element set {1812, 2012}
The set {∅}, whose only element is the empty set
No set at all, since a decision rule may never be false
questions.explanation: When a set is defined by a decision rule that is always false, the set is empty; no year is both ≥ 2012 and ≤ 1812, so the rule gives ∅, which is a different set from {∅}.

questions.prompt: For A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5}, what is the symmetric difference A ⊕ B?
questions.explanation: A ⊕ B = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B) = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} − {3, 4} = {1, 2, 5}, the elements that are in exactly one of the sets; {1, 2} is only the relative complement A − B.

questions.prompt: For A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {w, x, y, z}, how many elements does the Cartesian product A × B contain?
questions.explanation: |A × B| = |A| × |B| = 3 × 4 = 12 ordered pairs <a, b> with a ∈ A and b ∈ B; 7 would come from adding the cardinalities instead of multiplying them.

questions.prompt: Jorgensen says the fundamental difference between ordinary graphs and directed graphs is exactly the difference between which two notions?
options: Unordered pairs (a, b) versus ordered pairs <a, b>
Finite versus infinite sets of nodes
Union versus intersection of the edge sets
Total versus partial participation of the nodes
Subsets versus proper subsets of the node set
questions.explanation: For a ≠ b, (a, b) = (b, a) but <a, b> ≠ <b, a>; the book notes that this is exactly what separates ordinary (undirected) graphs from directed graphs.

questions.prompt: A partition of B is a set of subsets A1, …, An with A1 ∪ … ∪ An = B and i ≠ j ⇒ Ai ∩ Aj = ∅. Which two assurances do these two properties give testers?
options: Completeness and nonredundancy
Reflexivity and antisymmetry
Total and onto participation
Determinism and unambiguity
Closure and associativity
questions.explanation: The union condition guarantees completeness (every element is in some subset) and the disjointness condition guarantees nonredundancy (no element is in two subsets).

questions.prompt: The Triangle Program's universe (all triplets of positive integers) is split into equilateral, isosceles, scalene, right, and nontriangles. What problem does Jorgensen point out with this partition?
options: Scalene and right are not disjoint; the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is in both
The five subsets do not cover every triplet of positive integers
A partition of a set may contain at most four subsets
Nontriangles lie outside the universe of discourse
The right subset is empty, since no integer triplet forms a right triangle
questions.explanation: A partition needs pairwise disjoint subsets, but the 3, 4, 5 triangle is both scalene and right; the subsets still cover the whole universe, so coverage is not the issue.

questions.prompt: Let A = {date : 1 January 1812 ≤ date ≤ 31 December 2012}, B = {date : 2 January 1812 ≤ date ≤ 1 January 2013}, and C = A ∪ B. How does Jorgensen classify NextDate : A → C?
options: One-to-one and into
One-to-one and onto
Many-to-one and onto
Many-to-one and into
One-to-many and into
questions.explanation: Distinct dates have distinct next dates (one-to-one), but the image of A is B, a proper subset of C, so NextDate : A → C is into; NextDate : A → B is the one-to-one, onto case.

questions.prompt: Which statement about function types and testing does Jorgensen make?
options: One-to-one functions require much more testing than many-to-one functions
Many-to-one functions require much more testing than one-to-one functions
Into and onto functions need exactly the same domain- and range-based tests
A one-to-one, onto function has no inverse that could serve as a cross-check
Composed chains of functions are unproblematic once each function is tested
questions.explanation: The book says the into/onto distinction has implications for domain- and range-based functional testing and that one-to-one functions require much more testing than many-to-one functions; a one-to-one onto function always has an inverse usable as a cross-check.

questions.prompt: In a relation R ⊆ A × B, at least one element of A does not appear in any ordered pair of R. What is R's participation with respect to A?
options: Partial
Total
Onto
Into
One-to-many
questions.explanation: Participation is total if every element of A is in some ordered pair and partial otherwise (mandatory vs. optional participation); onto and into describe the same idea for the elements of B.

questions.prompt: Which combination of properties defines an ordering relation R ⊆ A × A?
options: Reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive
Reflexive, symmetric, and transitive
Symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive
Reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive
Symmetric and antisymmetric, but not reflexive
questions.explanation: An ordering relation (e.g., ≥ or Ancestor of) is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, whereas an equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

questions.prompt: Why do equivalence relations, and the partitions they induce, bring "great efficiency" to testing?
options: Testing one element of an equivalence class lets us assume the others behave similarly
Each element of the set must be tested once, in a fixed order
Overlapping classes let one test case cover several classes at once
Equivalence classes can only be the empty set or the whole universe
Antisymmetry guarantees that redundant test cases are detected automatically
questions.explanation: Partitions and equivalence relations are interchangeable, and great efficiency follows from testing just one element of an equivalence class and assuming the remaining elements behave similarly; equivalence classes never overlap.

questions.prompt: For which truth values of p and q is the IF-THEN proposition p → q false?
options: p is true and q is false
p is false and q is true
p is false and q is false
p is true and q is true
Whenever p and q have different truth values
questions.explanation: The IF-THEN truth table is T, F, T, T for (p, q) = TT, TF, FT, FF, so p → q is false only when p is true and q is false; "different truth values" describes exclusive-or.

questions.prompt: Which expression is logically equivalent to ¬((p → q) ∧ (q → p))?
options: p ⊕ q
p ↔ q
p ∧ q
p ∨ q
¬p ∧ ¬q
questions.explanation: The truth table of ¬((p → q) ∧ (q → p)) is F, T, T, F, identical to that of p ⊕ q; the un-negated (p → q) ∧ (q → p) is the bi-conditional p ↔ q.

questions.prompt: With Pr(p) = |T(p)| / |U| and U the set of the 12 months of a year, what is the probability of the proposition p(m): "m is a 30-day month"?
questions.explanation: The truth set T(p) is {April, June, September, November}, so Pr(p) = |T(p)| / |U| = 4/12; 11/12 would wrongly count every month with at least 30 days.
